content: 1. The solubility of atazanavir decreases as gastric pH increases. When antacids or buffered medications are co-administered, the plasma concentrations of atazanavir are expected to decrease. To mitigate this interaction, atazanavir should be administered either 2 hours before or 1 hour after these medications. 2. Atazanavir increases the levels or effects of capivasertib by inhibiting hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. If co-administration with strong CYP3A inhibitors cannot be avoided, the dose of capivasertib should be reduced, and patients should be monitored for adverse effects. 3. Atazanavir increases ceritinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. If co-administration is unavoidable, the ceritinib dose should be reduced by approximately 33%. After discontinuing the strong CYP3A inhibitor, the previous ceritinib dose should be resumed. 4. Chloramphenicol increases atazanavir levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. 5. Atazanavir increases the toxicity of cholic acid by reducing its elimination. Concomitant use of bile salt efflux pump (BSEP) inhibitors should be avoided, as this may exacerbate the accumulation of conjugated bile salts in the liver, leading to clinical symptoms. If co-administration is necessary, monitor serum transaminases and bilirubin levels. 6. Cimetidine decreases atazanavir levels by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. 7. H2-receptor antagonists (H2RAs) substantially reduce atazanavir plasma concentrations due to increased gastric pH. For treatment-naïve patients, atazanavir should be taken simultaneously with the H2RA or at least 10 hours afterward. For treatment-experienced patients, dosage adjustments should be made according to specific recommendations. 8. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) significantly reduce atazanavir plasma concentrations by increasing gastric pH. The PPI dose should not exceed a dose comparable to omeprazole 20 mg and must be taken approximately 12 hours before atazanavir/ritonavir in treatment-naïve patients. PPIs are not recommended for treatment-experienced patients taking atazanavir. 9. Atazanavir increases the levels or effects of cobicistat by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. 10. Atazanavir increases colchicine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors is contraindicated in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. If co-administration is necessary, the colchicine dose or frequency should be reduced as per prescribing information. 11. Atazanavir increases copanlisib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. If co-administration with strong CYP3A inhibitors cannot be avoided, the copanlisib dose should be reduced to 45 mg. 12. Atazanavir increases dabrafenib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. 13. Atazanavir increases daridorexant levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. 14. Dexlansoprazole decreases atazanavir levels by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. 15. Atazanavir increases dronedarone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 16. Efavirenz decreases atazanavir levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. 17. Atazanavir increases elacestrant levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. 18. Atazanavir increases elbasvir/grazoprevir levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 19. Atazanavir increases eluxadoline levels by inhibiting metabolism. If co-administered with OATP1B1 inhibitors, the eluxadoline dose should be reduced to 75 mg orally twice daily. 20. Atazanavir increases encorafenib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. If co-administration with a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor is unavoidable, the encorafenib dose should be reduced to one-third of the original dose. After discontinuing the inhibitor, the previous encorafenib dose should be resumed. 21. Atazanavir increases entrectinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors should be avoided. If unavoidable, the previous entrectinib dose should be resumed after discontinuing the inhibitor. 22. Enzalutamide decreases atazanavir levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 23. Atazanavir increases erdafitinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. If co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors is unavoidable, monitor closely for adverse reactions and consider dose adjustments. After discontinuing the inhibitor, consider increasing the erdafitinib dose if no drug-related toxicities are present. 24. Atazanavir increases ergoloid mesylates levels by inhibiting metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 25. Atazanavir increases ergotamine levels by inhibiting metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 26. Atazanavir increases erythromycin levels (base, ethylsuccinate, lactobionate, and stearate forms) by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 27. Esomeprazole decreases atazanavir levels by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. 28. Atazanavir increases everolimus levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration is contraindicated. 29. Famotidine decreases atazanavir levels by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. 30. Atazanavir increases fedratinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. If co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors is unavoidable, the fedratinib dose should be reduced to 200 mg/day. After discontinuing the inhibitor, the dose can be increased to 300 mg/day for 2 weeks, then to 400 mg/day as tolerated. 31. Atazanavir increases felbamate levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. 32. Atazanavir increases fentanyl levels (intranasal, transdermal, transmucosal) by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. If co-administration is necessary, monitor patients for respiratory depression and sedation at frequent intervals and consider fentanyl dose adjustments until stable drug effects are achieved. 33. Atazanavir decreases fexinidazole levels by inducing CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Conversely, fexinidazole increases atazanavir levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism, which may increase the risk of adverse effects. 34. Atazanavir increases fluticasone levels (intranasal) by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. Monitor for signs of systemic corticosteroid adverse effects, including Cushing-type symptoms. 35. Atazanavir increases gilteritinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If unavoidable, monitor closely for gilteritinib-related adverse effects and adjust dosage as needed. 36. Atazanavir increases glasdegib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If unavoidable, monitor for increased risk of adverse effects, including QTc interval prolongation. 37. Atazanavir increases glecaprevir/pibrentasvir levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 and OATP1B1 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided due to the increased risk of ALT elevations observed in clinical trials. 38. Atazanavir increases ibrutinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors should be avoided. If a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor must be used short-term (e.g., for ≤7 days), interrupt ibrutinib therapy until the inhibitor is discontinued. 39. Ibuprofen/famotidine decreases atazanavir levels by increasing gastric pH. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. 40. Atazanavir increases idelalisib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Co-administration should be avoided, or an alternative drug should be used. If co-administered, monitor for signs of idelalisib toxicity and adjust dosage as needed.
